newsitem.title: UK: Most suicides have executive lifestyle, study says.
newsitem.headline: Most suicides have executive lifestyle, study says.

text.p: Most people who commit suicide are deeply depressed, have been to doctors or counsellors but just cannot cope with the real world, right?
Wrong, a team of British psychologists said on Tuesday.
Most suicides are actually executive-type males who live alone, disregard doctors and do not want any help, Rory O'Connor and colleagues at Queen's University in Belfast said.
O'Connor told the annual conference of the British Psychological Society he had profiled three distinct personality types among people who had committed suicide, with surprising results.
Of the 142 people whose deaths he studied, 105 were men and 64 were what he called executive-type suicides.
"Executives are likely to be depressed, likely to be living alone and likely to be in employment, contrary to the traditional profile of suicide," O'Connor said.

But they were very unlikely to have seen their doctor recently or sought any type of help. "He is under stress and won't do anything about it and won't avail himself of the services there," O'Connor said.

The second group, the realists, tended to live alone and may have attempted suicide before. "They are highly unlikely to have visited a GP (doctor) or have a psychiatric history, but may have been hospitalised in the past," O'Connor said.
"They have a problem, they are under stress, but again they don't avail themselves of the help that is there."
The third group, which O'Connor calls psychiatric suicides, presents the "traditional" picture of suicide. Only 21 of the 142 suicides fell into this category.

"These individuals have had quite a hard life because they are alone, almost definitely have been hospitalised in the year prior, have visited their GP, are on medication, not in employment and have a previous history of attempts," he said.

O'Connor said his profiles, based on suicides in Northern Ireland, would be useful for psychologists everywhere because the province, despite its political unrest, has a typical European profile of suicide.
"What we have to do first is say "hold on a minute -- suicides aren't your typical psychiatric cases'," he said.

"A lot of males in particular aren't aware of the services available or the role of the GP (their family doctor). They feel quite embarrassed and feel they cannot express themselves. We have to de-stigmatise depression."
